vectors.description: A deceptive email impersonating a trusted sender to steal credentials or trigger a malicious action.
vectors.name: Phishing Email

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

Our payroll vendor migrated to a new system last night, and your salary details could not be carried over automatically. If you do not verify your bank account within 2 hours, this month's salary will be suspended.

Click here to verify immediately: http://nimbus-payroll-verify.net/login

Do not share this link with colleagues. Reply to this email with your employee ID if the link does not work.

Regards,
Priya Sharma
HR Department, {company}
flags: Sender domain nimbus-fintech-support.com is not the company domain
False urgency: your salary will supposedly be 'suspended in 2 hours'
Link uses plain http on an unrelated domain (nimbus-payroll-verify.net)
Asks you not to share the link with colleagues — real HR never does that
scenarios.subject: Action required: verify your {company} payroll details

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

This is an automated notice from the {company} Information Security team. Your domain password expires in 24 hours. After expiry you will lose access to email, VPN, and all internal tools until you visit the IT desk in person.

To avoid disruption, reset your password now using our secure portal:
https://sso-company-reset.com

This link is valid for 12 hours only. If you did not expect this message, please ignore it.

Regards,
Information Security
{company}
flags: Lookalike domain sso-company-reset.com is not the company domain
Threat of losing all access pressures you into a fast click
Real password resets happen inside the official SSO portal, not via emailed links
scenarios.subject: Your {company} password expires in 24 hours

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

As discussed in yesterday's review, I've shared the updated Q3 budget sheet with the revised {role} cost centres. Could you take a look and confirm the numbers by EOD?

https://docs-nimbusfintech.com/shared/budget-q3-final

The sheet includes the headcount changes we discussed for the {role} team, so your sign-off matters here. I know it's short notice, but Finance needs the locked version before tomorrow's leadership call.

Let me know if you can't open it and I'll resend it as an attachment.

Thanks,
Rahul
flags: Domain docs-nimbusfintech.com is a lookalike of the real nimbusfintech.com
No real prior context — the attacker bets you'll assume 'yesterday's review' happened
Unexpected external document link from a colleague who normally shares via the intranet
scenarios.subject: Re: Q3 budget review — shared doc

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

The IT team will perform scheduled maintenance on the corporate VPN this Sunday between 2:00 AM and 4:00 AM IST. During this window, VPN and intranet access will be intermittently unavailable.

No action is required from you. If you have critical work planned, please finish it before the window or contact the IT helpdesk on extension 4400.

You can track progress on our status page: https://status.nimbusfintech.com

Thank you for your patience,
{company} IT Operations
flags: Sent from the genuine company domain nimbusfintech.com
Asks for no credentials, no clicks on login links, no downloads
Points to the official status page and a helpdesk extension you can verify independently
scenarios.subject: Scheduled maintenance: VPN downtime Sunday 2-4 AM

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

This is a friendly reminder that the annual benefits enrolment window closes this Friday at 6 PM. If you have not yet selected your health insurance and meal-card options for next year, please do so here:

https://hr.nimbusfintech.com/enrolment

You will log in with your usual SSO — we will never ask for your password in an email. If you already enrolled, please ignore this message.

Questions? Write to people@nimbusfintech.com or drop by the HR desk on floor 4.

Best,
People Team, {company}
flags: Genuine company subdomain hr.nimbusfintech.com
Explicitly states passwords are never asked for in email
Verifiable offline at the HR desk on floor 4
scenarios.subject: Reminder: benefits enrolment closes Friday

vectors.description: A fraudulent text message manufacturing urgency to click a malicious link or share an OTP.
vectors.name: Smishing (SMS Phish)

scenarios.body: ALERT: Dear {player}, your salary account with {company}'s banking partner has incomplete KYC. As per RBI guidelines your account will be FROZEN within 6 hours and this month's salary credit will fail. Update your KYC immediately on this secure link: http://kyc-nimbus-verify.in/update Do NOT visit the branch — online update only. This is an automated message, so please do not call back on this number. Complete the update now to avoid any salary disruption this month. Reply STOP to opt out. -NIMBUS BANK
flags: Banks never ask you to complete KYC through an SMS link
A frozen-account threat is designed to create panic
Link uses plain http on a non-bank domain (kyc-nimbus-verify.in)
Real KYC happens inside the banking app or at a branch

scenarios.body: Hi {player}, your parcel from the {company} Rewards Store could not be delivered today due to an incomplete address. A redelivery fee of Rs 49 applies — pay within 24 hours or the parcel will be returned to sender: http://nimbus-courier.in/track Enter your UPI ID on the page to complete the payment. This is your final reminder — after 24 hours the parcel returns to sender and a fresh delivery fee will apply. Questions? Just reply to this SMS. -SwiftParcel Logistics
flags: A surprise fee for a parcel you never ordered
Payment demanded through a link instead of the courier's official app
Suspicious domain nimbus-courier.in — note the hyphen trick

scenarios.body: Hi {player}, this is the {company} IT Service Desk. We detected unusual sign-in attempts on your account from a new device in Hyderabad. To protect your account we are resetting your MFA enrolment. Please reply to this SMS with the 6-digit code you are about to receive, within the next 2 minutes. Do not share this code with anyone else. -IT Service Desk, {company}
flags: A real IT desk never asks you to text back an MFA code
The warning 'do not share this code' is social engineering — the attacker IS the recipient
Verify through the official IT helpline, never by replying to the SMS

scenarios.body: Dear {player}, Rs 48,500 has been credited to your salary account ending XX4521 on 24-Sep-2026 towards {company} payroll. Your available balance is Rs 52,310. If you do not recognise this transaction, please call our helpline on 1800-123-4567 immediately. Please remember: we never ask for your OTP, PIN, or CVV on a call or SMS. This is a system-generated message — please do not reply to this SMS. For any queries, write to care@nimbusbank.com or visit your nearest branch with a valid ID. -Nimbus Bank
flags: Purely informational — contains no link and asks you for nothing
Directs you to the official helpline printed on your debit card
Explicitly warns never to share OTPs — a genuine bank's habit

scenarios.body: Hi {player}, your SwiftParcel courier will arrive within the next 30 minutes with order #SP88412 from the {company} store. Please share the 4-digit OTP 7391 with the delivery agent ONLY at the time of handover to receive your parcel. Do not share this OTP with anyone over a phone call or SMS. If the OTP expires, the agent will generate a fresh one at your doorstep. For support, call SwiftParcel on 1800-419-7777 between 9 AM and 9 PM. Track your order: https://swiftparcel.in/t/88412
flags: The OTP is for in-person handover, and the message says so explicitly
It matches a delivery you are actually expecting
Sharing the OTP on a call is actively discouraged — the opposite of a scam SMS

vectors.description: A voice-phishing phone call impersonating IT support, a bank, or an authority figure.
vectors.name: Vishing Call

scenarios.body:
Caller: Good morning {player}, I'm calling from Nimbus Bank's fraud prevention team. We've detected a suspicious transaction of Rs 95,000 on your salary account that you did not authorise.
You: I didn't make any such transaction.
Caller: Don't worry, I can block it right away. For verification, please read out the OTP you just received on your phone, along with the CVV of your debit card.
You: ...
flags: A real bank never asks for your OTP or CVV on a call — not even its fraud team
The 'fraud alert' is crafted to panic you into cooperating
Hang up and call the number printed on the back of your card instead

scenarios.body:
Caller: Hi {player}, this is Arjun from {company} IT Support. Our monitoring shows your laptop is infected and is spreading malware across the office network right now.
You: What should I do?
Caller: Quick fix — I'm sending you a link to install a remote support tool so I can clean it up for you. Just open it, install, and read me the 9-digit code that appears on your screen.
You: ...
flags: Real IT support never cold-calls asking you to install remote-access software
Fear of infecting the whole network is meant to rush your judgement
Verify by calling the IT helpdesk extension yourself — never use their link

scenarios.body:
Caller: Hi {player}, I'm Meera from {company} HR. We're updating employee records for the new tax regime, and the PAN and Aadhaar details are missing from your {role} file.
You: Can't I just update this on the HR portal?
Caller: The portal sync is down this week, so I'm collecting details directly from employees. It will only take a minute — could you please confirm your PAN and the last 4 digits of your Aadhaar?
You: ...
flags: Sensitive ID documents are never collected over a phone call
The 'portal is down' excuse deliberately blocks the safe channel
A genuine HR drive like this would be announced by official email first

scenarios.body:
Caller: Hello {player}, this is the fraud team at Nimbus Bank. Did you just attempt a payment of Rs 12,400 to an electronics store in Pune?
You: Yes, that was me — I bought a monitor.
Caller: Thank you for confirming. No further action is needed and your card remains fully active. If anything looks unfamiliar later, please call the number on the back of your card.
You: Thanks, will do.
flags: Asks only to confirm a transaction — never your OTP, PIN, or CVV
The call ends without requesting any action from you
Directs you to the number on your card for anything further

scenarios.body:
Caller: Hi {player}, this is Kavita from the {company} IT helpdesk, calling back about ticket #48213 you raised this morning regarding VPN drops.
You: Yes, it's still disconnecting roughly every hour.
Caller: I can see your ticket notes here. Could you try connecting now and tell me what error code appears? I won't need your password at any point.
You: It says error 809.
Caller: Got it — I'll escalate this to the network team and update your ticket shortly.
flags: A callback you requested, tied to your genuine ticket #48213
The agent references details only the real helpdesk would know
Explicitly states your password will never be needed

vectors.description: A convincing replica of a real login page hosted on a lookalike domain.
vectors.name: Fake Login Portal

scenarios.body: NIMBUSFINTECH WEBMAIL — Secure Sign In. Welcome back, {player}. Please sign in with your company email address and password to access your inbox. [Email: ____] [Password: ____] [Sign In]. For the best experience, use Chrome or Edge. Never share your password with anyone — {company} IT will never ask for it. Last login: 23-Sep-2026, 09:14 AM from Pune. Forgot your password? Having trouble signing in? Contact IT support at support@nimbusfintech-login.tk. © 2026 NimbusFintech. All rights reserved.
flags: Address bar shows nimbusfintech-login.tk — a free domain, not the company site
No padlock or HTTPS on a page asking for your password
The support email uses the same fake domain
scenarios.subject: Sign in to NimbusFintech Webmail

scenarios.body: {company} SINGLE SIGN-ON. Sign in to continue to Outlook, Teams, and the HR Portal. [Work email] [Password] [Sign in]. For your security, enter the 6-digit code from your authenticator app after signing in. [Code] [Verify]. Your session is protected with 256-bit encryption. Signed in as {player}. Last successful sign-in: yesterday, 6:42 PM. If this wasn't you, contact IT Security immediately. This is a secure connection. Protected by NimbusFintech IT Security. Facing issues? Call extension 4400.
flags: Domain nimbusfintech-secure.com only mimics the real nimbusfintech.com
Harvesting your password AND authenticator code defeats MFA entirely
A genuine SSO page is reached via your bookmark or intranet — not a link
scenarios.subject: Single Sign-On — {company}

scenarios.body: Welcome to the {company} People Portal, {player}. Sign in with SSO to view payslips, apply for leave, and update your {role} profile. [Company email] [Password] [Sign In with SSO]. Your session is secure and encrypted. New here? Activate your account. This portal is maintained by the People Team. Having trouble? The People Team is available on chat support, Monday to Friday, 9 AM to 6 PM. For help, write to people@nimbusfintech.com. © 2026 {company}. Privacy | Terms | Accessibility.
flags: One-letter difference: nimbusfintech.co instead of nimbusfintech.com
Everything else looks perfect — that is exactly why this attack works
Always type the HR portal address yourself or use your saved bookmark
scenarios.subject: {company} HR Portal — Sign In

scenarios.body: {company} SINGLE SIGN-ON. Welcome, {player}. Sign in once to access email, VPN, and all company apps. [Work email] [Password] [Sign in]. Your authenticator app will now ask you to approve the sign-in — enter approval number 42 shown here. This page is managed by {company} IT. Never enter your password on any other sign-in page. Report suspicious pages to it-alerts@nimbusfintech.com.
flags: Genuine company domain sso.nimbusfintech.com served over HTTPS
MFA uses number-matching approval, not a typed code that can be relayed
You reached it through your own bookmark, not a link in a message
scenarios.subject: Single Sign-On — {company}

scenarios.body: Reset your {company} account password, {player}. Enter your work email below and we will send a one-time reset link, valid for 30 minutes. [Work email] [Send reset link]. Passwords must be at least 12 characters. You reached this page from the official IT helpdesk article 'Resetting your password'. If you did not request this, you can safely ignore it. Need help? Read the official guide linked from the intranet, or call the IT helpdesk on extension 4400.
flags: Genuine domain account.nimbusfintech.com
Only asks for your email — the reset link goes to your inbox, nothing is harvested here
Reached from an official helpdesk article, not an unexpected message
scenarios.subject: Reset your {company} password

vectors.description: An infected USB drive planted where an employee will find it and plug it in.
vectors.name: USB Drop

scenarios.body: You spot a plain black USB drive lying on the ground near the visitor parking area. It carries a handwritten sticker: 'CONFIDENTIAL — Q3 SALARY DATA — DO NOT SHARE'. There is no name, no asset tag, nothing identifying the owner. It looks like someone dropped it by accident this morning, and curiosity is doing the rest. A few colleagues have already gathered around it, debating whose it could be. Someone suggests plugging it into the spare laptop in the corner 'just to check the owner name'.
flags: Curiosity labels like 'CONFIDENTIAL SALARY DATA' are classic bait
No owner and no asset tag — untraceable by design
Rule: never plug in found media; hand it to IT or the security team
scenarios.from: Found on the ground near visitor parking, Block B
scenarios.subject: Unlabelled USB drive in the parking lot

scenarios.body: After the all-hands meeting you notice a sleek {company}-branded USB stick left behind on the conference table. A small tag reads 'Townhall photos + CEO address video'. It looks exactly like the giveaway drives from last year's Diwali event, and plugging it in would save you downloading the large video files from the intranet. The facilities team says lost property goes to the front desk, but nobody wants to walk all the way there. The drive is small enough to slip into a pocket 'for now'.
flags: Branding is cheap to fake — a sticker costs almost nothing
The helpful pretext ('save a download') gives you a reason to plug it in
Even real-looking event swag should go to IT for scanning first
scenarios.from: Found on the table after the all-hands meeting, Orion room
scenarios.subject: Branded USB stick left in the conference room

scenarios.body: You arrive on Monday morning to find a USB drive on your desk with an official-looking {company} asset tag: 'AST-22914 — Backup Drive'. A sticky note in familiar handwriting reads: 'Ran out of space on Friday — copied the {role} project backup here. - R'. The tag format matches real company assets, and it genuinely seems to be from a teammate.
flags: Attackers research asset-tag formats and teammate names to look internal
A 'helpful colleague' note manufactures trust and skips verification
Confirm with the teammate directly before ever connecting the drive
scenarios.subject: Spare drive left on your desk

scenarios.body: At the IT helpdesk you are issued a hardware-encrypted USB drive for transferring client data. The technician scans its serial number against your employee ID, has you set a PIN on the drive's own keypad, and gives you a signed custody form. The drive comes sealed in {company} IT packaging with a tamper-evident sticker intact. The technician also enables remote-wipe and shows you how to report the drive lost through the IT portal. The whole process takes about ten minutes.
flags: Issued face-to-face by IT with identity verification
Hardware encryption with a PIN you set yourself
Documented handover — the serial number is tied to your employee ID
scenarios.from: Handed over at the IT helpdesk, ground floor
scenarios.subject: New encrypted drive issued by IT

scenarios.body: Your onboarding kit includes a {company}-branded USB drive, factory-sealed in blister packaging, containing the employee handbook and IT setup guides. The welcome email from HR lists the exact contents of the kit, and the drive is read-only — it cannot be written to or executed from. You received the kit directly from the HR representative during orientation, along with your ID card and laptop.
flags: Factory-sealed and handed to you directly by HR
Read-only media cannot run malicious code
Contents match the inventory in your official welcome email
scenarios.from: Inside your Day-1 onboarding kit, received from HR
scenarios.subject: Sealed USB drive in the welcome kit

vectors.description: A QR code placed in a physical location that leads to a credential-harvesting page.
vectors.name: Malicious QR Code

scenarios.body: A glossy sticker is pasted over the cafeteria's printed menu: 'SCAN FOR TODAY'S FREE LUNCH COMBO — limited to the first 50 employees!' The QR code is large and colourful, and several colleagues are already scanning it. Scanning opens a page asking for your employee ID and date of birth to 'register your coupon'. The sticker edges are peeling — underneath, you can glimpse the original printed menu.
flags: Free-food urgency is designed to beat your scepticism
A sticker pasted OVER legitimate signage is a tampering red flag
No genuine coupon asks for your date of birth
scenarios.from: Stuck over the printed lunch menu near the counter
scenarios.subject: Sticker QR code in the cafeteria

scenarios.body: A neat printout on the IT notice board reads: 'Connect to Nimbus_Guest WiFi — scan to join instantly, no password needed!' The QR code is professionally printed on {company} letterhead. Scanning it would auto-configure a WiFi profile on your phone — but the network name in the fine print reads 'Nimbus_Guest_Free', which is not the official guest network name. The printout even carries a small 'Approved by IT' stamp at the bottom. Nobody remembers seeing an email about a new guest network, though.
flags: WiFi QR codes can silently install a malicious network profile on your phone
The network name differs slightly from the official one — check with IT
Genuine IT announcements about WiFi also arrive by official email
scenarios.from: Pinned on the IT notice board, 3rd floor
scenarios.subject: QR code for the new office WiFi

scenarios.body: The printed agenda for today's vendor review includes a QR code: 'Running late? Scan to join the meeting on Teams.' It looks like part of the official printout. Scanning it opens a pixel-perfect Teams sign-in page at teams-meetings-verify.com asking for your work email and password. The meeting organiser's laptop shows the same agenda on screen — but without any QR code.
flags: Attackers slip malicious QR codes into otherwise legitimate documents
The sign-in page sits on teams-meetings-verify.com, not microsoft.com
Compare with the organiser's on-screen copy — the QR code isn't there
scenarios.from: Handed out at the start of the vendor review meeting
scenarios.subject: QR code on the printed meeting agenda

scenarios.body: The table tents in the cafeteria carry a QR code: 'Rate today's lunch — 30 seconds, help us improve!' Scanning opens forms.nimbusfintech.com with a simple 5-question feedback form. It asks for no login and no personal details — just your meal rating and an optional comment. The same QR code appeared in the official cafeteria notice email sent last week.
flags: Leads to the genuine company domain forms.nimbusfintech.com
Asks for no login and no personal details
Matches the QR code in the official cafeteria email
scenarios.from: Printed on the table tents in the cafeteria
scenarios.subject: QR code for cafeteria feedback

scenarios.body: At reception, a tablet stand displays a QR code: 'Visiting {company}? Scan to check in.' Scanning opens checkin.nimbusfintech.com, where visitors enter their name and host employee. The receptionist confirms the same link is printed in the visitor policy, and the page shows the company's verified SSO badge. Employees never need to scan it — it's only for guests, and the receptionist walks visitors through it.
flags: Genuine checkin.nimbusfintech.com domain on a company-managed tablet
Only for visitors, supervised by the receptionist
Cross-checks with the printed visitor policy at the desk
scenarios.from: Displayed on the reception desk tablet stand
scenarios.subject: Visitor check-in QR at reception

vectors.description: A business email compromise: an urgent, confidential request impersonating a senior executive.
vectors.name: CEO Fraud (BEC)

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

I'm in back-to-back board meetings all day and need a quick favour. Could you buy 10 gift cards worth Rs 5,000 each from the store downstairs and send me the codes? They are for client Diwali gifts — very urgent.

I'll reimburse you today itself. The stores near the office sell them — please scratch the cards gently and send clear photos of the codes, front and back. I need this done before my 2 PM meeting. Please keep this between us for now.

Thanks,
A. Sharma
CEO, {company}
flags: The CEO is writing from a gmail address, not the company domain
Gift cards are a classic fraud payment method — untraceable
'Keep this between us' is designed to block verification
scenarios.subject: Urgent — need your help

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

We are closing the Meridian acquisition today and I need you to wire the advance of Rs 42,00,000 to the account details in the attached sheet. This is strictly confidential until the announcement — please do not discuss it with anyone, including Finance.

Confirm once done. This is time-sensitive: the window closes at 3 PM.

Regards,
A. Sharma
CEO
flags: Sender domain nimbusfintech-ops.com is not the company domain
Confidentiality pressure is used to bypass normal approvals
A genuine wire transfer always follows the documented approval workflow
scenarios.subject: Confidential wire — action by 3 PM

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

Per our discussion with Legal yesterday, please update TechServe Solutions' banking details in the vendor master to the account in the attached letter, and process their pending invoice of Rs 8,40,000 today.

I'm travelling with limited access — please reply to my personal email v.mehta.cfo@outlook.com to confirm. Finance is copied here, but please loop them out to avoid confusion.

Thanks,
Vikram
flags: Reply-to is a personal outlook.com address, not the CFO's official email
'Loop Finance out' removes the very people who would catch this
Vendor bank-detail changes always require dual verification under policy
scenarios.subject: Re: vendor payment — updated bank details

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

Could you please review the Q3 board deck when you get a chance? I've shared it on the company Drive — link inside. I'd appreciate your comments on the {role} section by Thursday EOD.

No rush beyond that — I know the release is keeping you busy. Happy to discuss on our 1:1 on Friday.

Thanks,
A. Sharma
flags: Sent from the genuine CEO address on the company domain
No secrecy and no manufactured urgency — a normal tone and timeline
Work happens on the shared Drive, verifiable in your regular 1:1
scenarios.subject: Please review: Q3 board deck (by Thursday)

scenarios.body:
Hi {player},

Invoice #INV-2291 from TechServe Solutions for Rs 8,40,000 is pending your approval as {role} budget owner. Please review and approve it in the procurement system:
https://procure.nimbusfintech.com/approvals

This follows the standard two-step approval — Priya from Finance has already verified the PO. The payment run is on Friday, so nothing is urgent. You can view the PO, the invoice scan, and the full approval history under the 'Documents' tab before you decide. The system logs every action for audit.

Thanks,
Finance Team
flags: The request flows through the official procurement system, not email instructions
Two-step approval with Finance verification already completed
No confidentiality pressure — everything is documented and traceable
scenarios.subject: Payment approval needed: TechServe invoice #INV-2291

vectors.description: A fake update prompt that installs malware when accepted.
vectors.name: Fake Software Update

scenarios.body: WARNING! Your Adobe Flash Player is OUTDATED. 3 viruses have been detected on this device! Your files are at RISK. Click UPDATE NOW to install Flash Player 32 and clean your system instantly. [UPDATE NOW] [Remind me later]. Do NOT close this window — closing it may damage your files permanently! Your Windows Defender has been disabled by the threat! Only Flash Player 32 can remove these infections. 1,247 users updated in the last hour. Act now to stay protected!
flags: Flash Player was discontinued in 2020 — no genuine update exists
Scare tactics: fake virus counts and threats of file damage
Real updates never arrive as popups on a web page
scenarios.subject: Your Flash Player is OUTDATED

scenarios.body: A blue fullscreen message appears: 'A critical security update is available for your device. Your system will restart in 5:00 minutes. [Install update now] [Postpone]. To install faster, download the update assistant: windows-update-assistant.net/setup.exe'. The countdown timer keeps ticking, and the usual Windows Update settings page is nowhere to be found. This update includes critical patches for 14 vulnerabilities. Your IT administrator has approved this update. Do not turn off your device during installation.
flags: Genuine Windows updates install through Settings — never via a downloaded .exe
A countdown timer pressures you to act without thinking
The download domain windows-update-assistant.net is not Microsoft
scenarios.subject: Critical Security Update Available

scenarios.body: Your {company} VPN client shows a notification: 'A required security update (v4.2.1) is available. You must update before connecting — your current version will stop working today.' The popup's design, logo, and fonts match the real VPN client perfectly. [Update now] [Details]. Clicking 'Details' opens a changelog hosted on vpn-update-nimbus.com. Release notes: fixes connection drops on Windows 11, improves reconnect speed by 40 percent, and patches a security flaw. Update size: 86 MB. Estimated install time: 2 minutes.
flags: The changelog link points to vpn-update-nimbus.com, not the company domain
Forced-update pressure: 'will stop working today'
Real client updates come through the company's Software Center, not in-app popups
scenarios.from: VPN client notification on your laptop
scenarios.subject: Nimbus VPN — update required

scenarios.body: The {company} Software Center — the IT-managed app on your laptop — shows 3 pending updates: the VPN client, endpoint security, and Office. Each update lists its publisher, version number, and release notes. You click Install, the updates apply silently in the background, and a toast notification confirms completion. No browser windows, no downloads, no countdown timers. You opened Software Center yourself from the Start menu, as the IT onboarding guide showed.
flags: You opened the IT-managed Software Center yourself
Each update lists a verified publisher and release notes
No urgency, no external downloads, no countdown timers
scenarios.subject: Software Center: 3 updates ready

scenarios.body: Your browser's menu shows a small 'Update' badge. Opening it reads: 'A new version is available. Restart the browser to apply the update — your tabs will be restored.' You click Restart, the browser updates in a few seconds, and the About page confirms the new version number. The entire flow stays inside the browser you already trust, with no downloads from external sites.
flags: The prompt lives inside the browser's own menu — not on a web page
No external downloads; your tabs are restored automatically
The new version is verifiable on the browser's About page
scenarios.from: Your web browser's own update prompt
scenarios.subject: Update available — restart to apply
